task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: causal effect of opponent next-possession PPP on AVOID labels
relationship between own-sequence lags and play-type labeling

historical_evidence.finding: A specific opponent play type on the preceding possession suppresses each star's next-possession PPP relative to that star's baseline. PUTBACK is top suppressor for 6+ stars; other tops include TRANSITION and POST_UP. Sample sizes 32–95 for PUTBACK cells; no multiplicity correction. Validation not recorded.
Specific opposing lineups, defenders, play types and preceding opponent play types suppress star efficiency. Rank‑1 deltas within 1–2 SE; no multiple‑comparison control; other artifacts noted.

Play‑type PPP differences are largely artifacts of labeling and foul leakage: OTHER PPP inflated 36% by fouls, DRIVE PPP 12pp below foul benchmark. Only 0.7% of possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type.

Opponent's previous play type changes your next‑possession PPP after matching on defensive team. Three cells survive multiple controls (SPOT_UP→TRANSITION, POST_UP→TRANSITION, PNR→DRIVE) but most of 64 cells are null.

failed_approaches.what_failed: small sample size and lack of multiplicity correction
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear), n_after=32–95, no validation recorded.

failed_approaches.what_failed: no multiple‑comparison control and unclear mechanism

failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by labeling flaw).

evidence_establishes: There is evidence that opponent play type can suppress a star's next‑possession PPP in some cases. Some opponent‑action effects survive defensive matching and prior‑made‑shot controls. Labeling artifacts exist that can inflate PPP differences.
evidence_does_not_establish: A general causal effect of opponent next‑possession PPP on AVOID labels for all play types. The magnitude and consistency of the effect across teams, seasons, and play‑type categories remain uncertain. No robust validation of the findings.
own_inferences: The data contain labeling artifacts and limited sample sizes for many play‑type cells, which could bias results. Defensive quality and opponent lineup mismatches may confound the estimated effect. Non‑stationarity across seasons may further threaten validity.
uncertainties: Whether the identified suppression effects generalize beyond the few cells found. Whether the labeling artifact identified in [prior work]‑025 fully explains the observed PPP differences. The extent to which defensive matching adequately removes confounding.

historical_effect.explanation: Historical evidence shows both potential effects and serious methodological issues (labeling artifacts, small samples, lack of controls). This requires a more rigorous design before proceeding.

blocking_constraints.text: Limited sample sizes for many play‑type cells reduce power.
Defensive match quality and opponent lineup may confound the effect.
Seasonal changes could affect play‑type distributions.
Many play‑type comparisons without correction risk false positives.

prior_work.summary: Previous studies identified some opponent‑play effects on star PPP and highlighted labeling artifacts, but none provide a comprehensive, validated causal test of opponent next‑possession PPP on AVOID labeling across all play types.

risks.text: Small n for many play‑type cells.
Labeling and foul leakage distort PPP.
Defense quality and opponent lineups confound effects.

design.estimand: Average causal effect of opponent next‑possession PPP on the probability of an AVOID label for a given play type, conditional on own‑sequence lags and defensive matching.
design.sample: All possessions in NBA 2022‑2026 seasons that have a clearly labeled initial play type and recorded next‑possession PPP.
design.power: Target 80% power to detect a standardized effect size of 0.20, requiring ~2000 observations per cell after matching and controlling for covariates.
design.controls: Defensive match 8x8 (opponent lineup), previous made shot, opponent play type, own play type, period, score differential, and season fixed effects.
design.falsification: Test the same causal model on randomly selected play types where no theoretical effect is expected (e.g., play types with historically neutral PPP).
design.multiplicity: Apply Benjamini‑Hochberg FDR control across the pre‑specified set of play‑type comparisons; pre‑register the test set of hypotheses.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null hypothesis for a cell if the estimated effect is significant at p<0.05 after FDR correction.
design.data_version: NBA 2022‑2026 season per‑game play‑by‑play data, with play‑type possession records constructed via the existing graph database.
